item.title: Full text: Keynote speech by Chinese Premier Li Qiang at opening ceremony of 140th session of China Import and Export Fair
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 15:33:00
Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Wednesday delivered a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the 140th session of China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province. Please see the attachment for the English version of the full text of the address. Keynote Speech by H.E. Li Qiang Premier of the State Council of the People's Republic of China At the Opening Ceremony of the 140th Session of China Import and Export Fair Guangzhou, October 14, 2026 Distinguished Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, Friends, It is a great pleasure to join you in the beautiful Flower City Guangzhou for the 140th Session of China Import and Export Fair (Canton Fair). On behalf of the Chinese government, I would like to extend a warm welcome to you all, and express heartfelt appreciation for your long-standing, positive contribution to the economic and trade cooperation and development between China and other countries. This year marks the 70th anniversary of the Canton Fair. President Xi Jinping has sent a congratulatory letter to the Fair, acknowledging its past achievements and reaffirming China's commitment to expanding high-standard opening up. Over the past 70 years, the Canton Fair has grown from strength to strength. Its exhibition area has expanded from 9,600 square meters in the first year to 1.55 million square meters today. The number of buyers has increased from 1,200 in the beginning to more than 300,000 this year. Among all the international trade exhibitions hosted by China, the Canton Fair has the longest history, the largest participation and the highest transaction volume. It is also an important window for the international community to observe China. Through this window, the world has witnessed the surging vitality of China's economy and society, the enterprising journey undertaken by hundreds of millions of Chinese people, and the deepening connection between China and the world. First, a China that keeps opening itself creates new opportunities for the world. Over the past 70 years, the Canton Fair has established itself and thrived on openness. Its circle of friends has grown bigger, with buyers coming from over 220 countries and regions, and the total value of business deals reaching US$1.6 trillion. What underlies this success is China's strategic choice of boosting development through openness, and the practical need for countries around the world to leverage their economic strengths for mutual empowerment. China is now a key trading partner of over 160 countries and regions, and the top export destination for nearly 80 countries and regions. China's stock of overseas investment has reached US$3.4 trillion. While developing itself, China has also brought benefits to the world. Second, a China that keeps innovating itself provides new impetus for the world. Over the past 70 years, exhibits at the Canton Fair have been continuously transformed and upgraded. From agricultural and subsidiary products and local specialties in the 1960s and 70s, to industrial and electromechanical products in the 1980s and 90s, and to embodied artificial intelligence (AI) and smart medical services today, each session of the Canton Fair presents an updated selection of exhibits. What underlies this transformation is China's rapid progress in innovation-driven development, and the world's scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation. In recent years, new technologies, products and business forms in such areas as AI, green energy and biomedicine have continued to emerge in China, and generated new dynamism and space for the world economy. Third, a China that always keeps its promise brings certainty to the world. Over the past 70 years, no matter how the international situation evolved, the Canton Fair has never been interrupted, and its commitment to the principle of honoring contracts and maintaining credibility remains steadfast. What underlies such commitment is the Chinese philosophy of matching words with actions, and the world's recognition of and trust in China. China has all along kept its policies stable and consistent, firmly delivered on its commitment of lowering tariffs, increasing development assistance and addressing climate change, and undertaken the responsibilities of a major country in this turbulent and changing world. Looking back on the past 70 years, the Canton Fair has stood the test of international vicissitudes and brimmed with new vigor and vitality. This is because it has all along followed the trend of economic globalization and answered the call of the international community for joint development. The journey of the Canton Fair offers some simple yet profound takeaways worthy of deep reflection. Here, I would like to share with you three main observations. First, market connectivity is not a tool for zero-sum games between countries, but an effective measure to foster new space for growth. The past few years have seen a notable rise in manmade market barriers of various sorts around the globe. Some have even chosen to politicize, instrumentalize, and weaponize economic and trade issues. However, no matter their forms, protectionism is always at the core. It has been fully proven by both theories and practices that the market is not static—it is more like a network that reaches out in all directions. Only when connected to more such networks, can a market achieve economy of scale, match supply with demand more efficiently, and create more value and space. Protectionism may seem effective for a country to sustain its market, but it also makes it impossible for the country to broaden its market. Worse still, it may even lose its place in the new global network of markets. At the end of the day, protectionism will only produce more losses than gains. Throughout the years, China has been committed to integrating its domestic market with the international markets for joint growth. China has been the second largest importer in the world for 17 consecutive years, exceeding RMB 18 trillion yuan last year, and growing by another 22.3 percent in the first three quarters this year. Decades have passed since China opened itself to the world, yet its market has not contracted. Instead, the introduction of new products and industries from other countries, such as automobiles and home appliances, has unlocked and cultivated new market demands. Meanwhile, the export of quality Chinese products, especially innovative products, is opening up new space for the global marketplace. China is ready to work with all countries to build an open world economy and strengthen market connectivity so as to make the global market bigger and deliver greater benefits to all. Second, international trade is not just statistics in the books, but a voluntary choice aimed to improve people's well-being. Recently, there have been quite some discussions about the issue of trade balance globally. The laws of economics tell us that a balanced position in trade is temporary and relative, while an imbalanced position is more common and non-static. This is determined by countries' differences in comparative strengths, economic structures, distribution of labor, and other variables. We need to see that trade is mutually beneficial in nature. One cannot simply view surplus as "taking advantage" and deficit as "being ripped off." A balanced trade would naturally arrive when the parties can satisfy their respective demands through positive interactions. It is not achieved by building walls, setting up barriers, or even suppressing and containing others. It is simply unrealistic to impose export control on others while looking for balanced trade at the same time. Such a practice will only push up costs, disrupt industrial and supply chains, and further aggravate the imbalance. What we need is "upward balance" achieved by opening up wider and making the economic pie bigger, not "downward balance" resulting from market closure and the inevitable market contraction that follows. Some current discussions about China's trade focus on import and export statistics, but overlook the real effects behind them. China is both a "super seller" and a "super buyer." As a "super seller," China brings benefits to its trading partners. Quality, affordable goods made by diligent Chinese workers with their labor and wisdom have significantly increased the actual purchasing power of global consumers, improved their quality of life, and helped countries strengthen their capacity for industrial development. As a "super buyer," China helps to boost the prosperity of other countries. China is a major buyer of agricultural, industrial, and consumer goods from many countries, which translate into profits for local businesses, income for the people, and revenues for the governments. China never seeks surplus intentionally, not to mention the fact that most of the times, the benefits are shared by all parties, despite the surplus being recorded in China. A large number of foreign-invested enterprises in China export their products across the world and secure big returns. We would like to buy more products from across the world, especially high value-added products. Since last year, we have hosted around 70 events themed "Big Market for All: Export to China." Next month, we will host the ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai. China hopes that more countries will work together in the same direction, lift restrictions, and pursue better, balanced development of trade. Third, win-win cooperation does not mean one-sided concession but mutual empowerment and success. On the path toward global prosperity and development, win-win cooperation is the only right choice. A zero-sum approach hurts everybody. For true win-win cooperation to happen, we cannot rely on a simple quid pro quo, still less compromise or concessions under pressure. What we need is to treat each other as equals, meet each other halfway, and make progress together. With all the links of global industrial and supply chains interlocked and closely connected, it is possible to realize more sustainable win-win cooperation at a higher level if countries work together in good faith and draw on each other's strengths. In this process, developed countries should take more proactive actions, provide developing countries with more capital and technological support and preferential economic and trade policies to help boost their industries and strengthen the internal drivers of growth. China, as the largest developing country, is committed to advancing common development. While developing itself, China has done its utmost to help and support other developing countries. Over the years, China has been advancing high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. More and more fellow developing countries, supported by China's products, technology and capital, have improved their domestic industrial systems, raised high-end export capacity, kept accelerating industrial upgrade, and as a result, continued to move up the global value chain. There are over 50,000 overseas companies set up with Chinese investments, 90 percent of which are in Global South countries. Many of these countries have seen their manufacturing rapidly growing and foreign exchange earnings from exports rising significantly. China will always be a good friend that other developing countries can trust and rely on. China stands ready to help pave the way for other developing countries as they pursue modernization. We will join hands and move forward together with fellow developing countries. Over the years, China has been actively carrying out global open cooperation and made important contribution to meeting the world's needs with its utmost efforts. This year, confronted with global changes and turbulence, the Chinese economy has withstood pressure and forged ahead steadily, demonstrating robust resilience and vitality. We are confident and capable of accomplishing the goals and tasks for economic and social development this year. China will continue to advance high-quality development, expand high-standard opening up, and take more practical actions to inject more momentum into the world economy. First, we will share more market opportunities. The demand of China's supersized market is unleashing at a faster pace. Last year, total retail sales of consumer goods exceeded RMB 50 trillion yuan for the first time, and are expected to increase by about another RMB 10 trillion yuan in the next five years. We will firmly implement the strategy of expanding domestic demand and advance consumption upgrade, further lower the threshold of market access, and provide better services and safeguards for enterprises. We welcome more foreign companies to do business in China. Second, we will expand more mutually beneficial cooperation. China is committed to pursuing progress together with the world and deepening alignment of development strategies with other countries. We support capable Chinese companies in investing overseas in an orderly manner, strengthening technological exchanges, expanding cooperation in emerging sectors, and conducting more localized operations, to help upgrade local industries and boost local economy. Third, we will firmly uphold international economic and trade order. China will always stand on the right side of history, firmly uphold multilateralism and free trade, and support WTO reform and development. We will work with all parties to explore and make future-oriented international economic and trade rules, reform and improve global economic governance, and advance a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization. Seven decades of hard work have yielded fruitful results. I believe the Canton Fair will make new and even better progress going forward. I hope that you will make more friends here, carry out more cooperation, and reap more fruits. Let us work together to usher in a better future. Thank you.

item.title: China ready to continue facilitating review, approval of rare-earth export licenses to Europe, urges reciprocation: MOFCOM
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 15:30:00
MOFCOM spokesperson He Yadong Photo: Tao Mingyang/GT China stands ready to continue facilitating the review and approval of rare-earth export licenses to Europe, and hopes the European side will reciprocate by facilitating the resolution of key individual cases concerning licenses for Chinese entities in the dual-use field, China's Ministry of Commerce spokesperson He Yadong said on Thursday, responding to a question about rare-earth export licenses to the EU. "China will work with the European side to keep leveraging the export control dialogue mechanism and promote the growth of bilateral trade in dual-use items," He said.

item.title: New China-DPRK border bridge over Yalu River opens to traffic
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 14:49:00
An opening ceremony is held for a new bridge across the Yalu River, the border river of China and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), on Oct. 15, 2026. (Photo: Xinhua) An opening ceremony is held for a new bridge across the Yalu River, the border river of China and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), on Oct. 15, 2026. (Photo: Xinhua) This photo taken on Oct. 15, 2026 shows a new bridge across the Yalu River, the border river of China and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). The opening ceremony for the new China-DPRK border bridge over Yalu River was held on Thursday. (Photo: Xinhua) The new China-DPRK Yalu River bridge officially opened to traffic on Thursday, with both sides jointly holding an opening ceremony on this cross-border artery. The cable-stayed bridge over the Yalu River serves as a cross-border transport link between the city of Dandong in northeast China's Liaoning Province and the city of Sinuiju in North Pyongan Province in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). The double-pylon and double-cable-plane bridge features a 28.5-meter-wide deck designed with four lanes for two-way traffic, while its water navigation clearance is designed for vessels of up to the 3,000-tonne class. The new bridge will further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday. China and the DPRK are friendly neighbors connected by mountains and rivers, and the new bridge is an important facility for connectivity between the two countries, Mao noted at a regular press briefing. Dandong boasts China's largest border trade port with the DPRK. Before the new road bridge, the Yalu River Bridge, also known as the China-DPRK Friendship Bridge, served as a combined road-rail bridge. The old one, however, could only accommodate trucks weighing no more than 20 tonnes for one-way road traffic. China and the DPRK in 2010 agreed to build a new road bridge downstream from the old one.

item.title: ASML calls US restrictions on DUV sales to China counterproductive; stance reflects strategic dilemma amid pressure: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 13:32:00
ASML Photo: VCG Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML has pushed back against a US Congress proposal seeking to further restrict its sales of deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines to China, saying that such measures would do more harm than good and could speed up China’s drive to develop homegrown alternatives. Chinese experts said the remarks underscore the complex calculations facing the company as global semiconductor competition intensifies, and reflect the strategic dilemma ASML faces amid pressure from US restrictions. On a call with reporters following the release of the company's third-quarter results, ASML’s Chief Financial Officer Roger Dassen said the passage of the US MATCH Act would speed up China's domestic development of competing technology, Reuters reported on Wednesday. During the earnings call, ASML’s Chief Executive Officer Christophe Fouquet also noted that demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment in China remains strong, supported by domestic investment in chip production, with continued construction of wafer fabrication plants expected to support demand in 2027 and beyond. ASML expects China to account for about 20 percent of its total sales this year, according to financial results released on Wednesday. Xiang Ligang, director-general of the Zhongguancun Modern Information Consumer Application Industry Technology Alliance, told the Global Times on Thursday that ASML’s strong quarterly results were primarily supported by the ongoing expansion of advanced manufacturing capacity fueled by artificial intelligence demand, which has kept orders for high-end lithography equipment elevated. The ASML’s stance reflects a strategic dilemma shaped by multiple external pressures, Ma Jihua, a veteran tech industry analyst, told the Global Times on Thursday. The company is currently navigating a complex balancing act in its China market strategy: while seeking to expand their presence in China, they must also respond to US policies and demands, he said. The Dutch company faces growing competition from China’s semiconductor sector and related equipment manufacturers, which are accelerating efforts to develop and manufacture critical tools such as lithography machines domestically, Xiang said, adding that as China’s domestic lithography equipment industry gradually becomes more competitive between 2028 and 2030, the market landscape could undergo significant changes. According to Xiang, AI development is generating demand across computing centers, servers, robots, smart vehicles and other areas. Chinese chips are increasingly serving these markets, supported by their ability to meet diverse requirements and their competitive pricing. Ma also pointed out that although US restrictions have, in the short term, limited the flow of some advanced equipment and processes into China, they have not stopped Chinese tech firms from continuing to advance in mature-node manufacturing, equipment replacement, and independent innovation. Chinese semiconductor companies are also expected to post strong revenue growth. Citing data from industry information platform chinadatapay.com, the Securities Times reported that consensus forecasts put the combined 2026 revenue of 146 A-share-listed semiconductor companies at 1.24 trillion yuan, up more than 70 percent on a comparable basis. The strong performance of China's chip industry is also reflected in export data. China's integrated-circuit exports reached $256.75 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up 103.9 percent year-on-year, according to customs data cited by the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products. The chamber also reported a 95.8 percent increase in average export unit value.

item.title: Jurassic bird discovery by Chinese scientists challenges classic avian evolution view
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 11:33:00
A skeletal reconstruction of Yangyuanornis Photo: Courtesy of Wang Min Chinese researchers have identified a new Jurassic bird fossil - a discovery that challenges the conventional notion that the origin and early evolution of birds were primarily driven by adaptations for flight, according to a report released by the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences on Wednesday. The new findings confirmed that ecological specialization for ground-dwelling and flightlessness had already emerged in the earliest stages of bird evolution. The new species also exhibits a striking combination of dinosaur-like and bird-like morphological features, researchers said. The research results, conducted by a team led by researcher Wang Min at the IVPP in collaboration with the Institute of Geological Sciences in East China's Fujian Province, were published on Nature on Wednesday. The discovery fills a critical gap in the temporal and evolutionary record of birds. As the earliest known flightless bird, it challenges the hypothesis of a unidirectional evolutionary trajectory toward flight, demonstrating that the evolution of the avian body plan did not follow a single, linear path toward improved flight capabilities, but instead involved a complex process of rapid ecological exploration, Wang said. The new bird was named Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis , after Yangyuan township in Fujian, where the fossil was discovered. The second part of the name is derived from a mythical bird in ancient Chinese legends. It lived during the Late Jurassic period (150 million-148 million years ago), according to the report. Researchers found that the new species fell outside the groups of tree-dwelling, aquatic and wading birds, instead clustering within the overlapping region of modern ground-dwelling birds and flightless birds. Combined with features such as a relatively wide angle between the clavicles and a trapezoidal coracoid, the findings indicate that it was a flightless, carnivorous bird adapted for running on land, the report said. The transition from terrestrial dinosaurs to flying birds is one of the most remarkable events in the history of life. Macroevolutionary models suggest that birds originated and underwent their early diversification during the Jurassic. However, the fossil record of birds from this pivotal geological period remains extremely sparse, leaving scientists without clear fossil evidence of how the characteristic avian body plan emerged, the report said. For decades, a prevailing view has been that selection pressures associated with flight was the dominant force driving morphological evolution in early birds. Yet gaps in the fossil record at critical phylogenetic and chronological junctures have limited scientists' understanding of the evolutionary pathways and ecological diversity of birds in the earliest stages of their history, said the report.

item.title: India's 'victory narrative' will only hit a wall on China-India border: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 23:51:00
China, India Illustration: GT By changing a few place names, creating some media hype, it projects a tough stance and creates the illusion that its territorial claims have been realized on the ground. Such petty scheming is, at its core, nothing more than psychological victory in the absence of real gains - a manifestation of the self-deluding "victory narrative" embraced by some in India, now projected onto the China-India boundary issue. Some people in India are once again playing games with maps over the China-India border issue. Recently, India's Ministry of Home Affairs announced what it called the "standard names" for 28 locations in the so-called "Union Territory of Ladakh" and marked them on official Indian maps. Some of these locations lie in areas on the western sector of the China-India border that are under China's actual control. Including the 27 locations in China's Zangnan, Southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, that India illegally renamed unilaterally in August this year, India has forcibly slapped an "Indian label" on 55 locations along the China-India border in just two months. This tactic is nothing new. First comes an administrative announcement, followed by the names being entered on official maps, and then repeated amplification through the media. The intent is not hard to discern: India hopes that, at minimal cost, it can gradually shape perceptions of the boundary issue among its own public and the international community, dressing up its unilateral claims as so-called "established facts." By changing a few place names, creating some media hype, it can project a tough stance and create the illusion that its territorial claims have been realized on the ground. Such petty scheming is, at its core, nothing more than psychological victory in the absence of real gains - a manifestation of the self-deluding "victory narrative" embraced by some in India, now projected onto the China-India boundary issue. Naming a place cannot directly create territorial sovereignty, and a map is no final ruling on territorial sovereignty. In 2019, India unilaterally amended its domestic laws, revoked relevant constitutional provisions, and announced the creation of the so-called "Union Territory of Ladakh," deliberately incorporating Chinese territory in the western sector of the China-India border into its own administrative jurisdiction. China made its opposition clear at the time, and its position has remained firm and consistent ever since. If a country could simply pass a law unilaterally declaring its neighbor's territory to be its own, there would be no need for countries around the world to negotiate their border disputes. They could settle everything from behind a desk by redrawing maps, issuing notices, and stamping official documents. So, India's actions are unacceptable and have no legal effect. The status quo along the Ladakh sector of the boundary is not a blank sheet of paper that can be altered at will. The western sector of the China-India border has historically belonged to China, and China possesses sovereignty over the relevant areas, including Aksai Chin region in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, and has ample historical and legal grounds for its claims. India's claims stem from illegal boundary demarcations inherited from the colonial era, which successive Chinese governments have never recognized. This is precisely why India's place-naming move, designed purely to assert sovereignty and expand its claims on maps, is fundamentally different from China's lawful standardization of place names in Zangnan. Chinese territory will not become Indian simply because India assigns it a name. Such wishful thinking does nothing to help resolve the China-India boundary issue properly. The boundary issue has a bearing on the overall relationship between the two countries, and New Delhi also frequently speaks of the situation on border areas. When Prime Minister Narendra Modi met with Chinese leader in September this year, he called on the two countries to jointly safeguard peace and tranquility in the border areas. Earlier, India's ambassador to China, Vikram Doraiswami, wrote in the Global Times that peace and tranquility along the China-India border would help promote partnership and cooperation between the two sides. If that is indeed the case, India should exercise greater restraint on issues of this kind rather than provoke tensions. Some Indian politicians are now keen to stage political shows over the border issue to divert attention from domestic problems and pander to nationalist sentiment. Such behavior will only erode mutual trust between the two, do nothing to resolve the dispute, and create fresh obstacles to the improving China-India relationship. Ultimately, the negative consequences will also be borne by India itself. For years, China and India have maintained communication through channels such as meetings between their special representatives on the boundary question, making sustained efforts to manage differences and advance negotiations. The hard-won peace and tranquility in border areas deserve to be jointly safeguarded. China and India are important neighbors, major developing countries, and representatives of emerging economies. Their relationship extends beyond the bilateral sphere and carries global and strategic significance. Greater cooperation between the two countries within multilateral frameworks, including the United Nations, BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, and the G20, is vital to addressing global challenges and upholding international fairness and justice. India should work with China in the same direction and approach bilateral relations with a strategic vision and a long-term perspective, using the political wisdom of mutual respect and understanding to overcome disturbances. China's commitment to improving and developing relations with India remains unchanged. We urge India to act in the broader interests of bilateral relations, exercise prudence in both words and actions on the boundary issue, and follow the important understandings reached by the two countries' leaders. India should strictly honor the relevant agreements between the two sides and take concrete steps to create a favorable environment for improving and developing bilateral relations, rather than take actions that further complicate the boundary issue. No unilateral move to alter the status quo can shake China's firm resolve to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity, nor can it change the objective facts long established by history and the realities on the ground.

item.title: GT Voice: How Asia could benefit from AI-driven expansion of trade
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 22:55:00
AI Illustration: Chen Xia/Global Times The IMF's new chief economist Silvana Tenreyro said on Tuesday that global trade grew 8.3 percent between 2023 and 2025, while global trade in AI grew by 29 percent, benefiting China, India and other Asian countries, Reuters reported. Why has Asia reaped the benefits of the expansion of AI trade? First, AI depends heavily on hardware. Chip manufacturing, server assembly, data center construction and power infrastructure all require a mature industrial system, large-scale manufacturing capacity and a stable supply chain network as their foundation. After decades of industrial upgrading and technological accumulation, the capacity and cost advantages in these segments have long been concentrated in Asia. From memory chip manufacturing to the ecosystem covering advanced processes, server components and cooling systems, to the large-scale production capacity of servers, optical modules and electronic components, Asia has formed the world's most complete AI hardware supply network. In the first eight months of this year, China's exports of servers, optical modules and electronic components grew at double-digit rates year-on-year, while its share of global humanoid robot shipments rose to 97 percent, according to customs statistics. Behind these figures lies the supply capacity that Asian manufacturing has unleashed in the AI hardware sector. Second is the scale effect on the demand side. China and India combined have more than 2.8 billion people, a regional market without parallel anywhere else in the world. It serves as both a vast proving ground for AI applications and a mega-buyer of AI hardware and services. In Asia, AI demand is being released simultaneously across countless scenarios, such as AI-assisted product selection for cross-border e-commerce livestreams, image recognition built into educational devices, and AI-powered quality inspection on factory floors. Feedback from hundreds of millions of users feeds back into product iteration at a speed unmatched elsewhere. This is what AI adoption in Asia looks like: not confined to laboratories or launch events, but reaching into every capillary of commerce, manufacturing and daily consumption. That endogenous demand is itself a key pillar of global AI trade. Some may be wondering whether Asia's deep participation in the AI cycle comes at the expense of advanced economies. The answer is no. Asia's AI-driven growth is not about taking dividends away from them. It is about making the global AI pie larger by providing manufacturing capacity and market space. Asian factories supply computing equipment to the world, and Asian markets provide revenue and users to global AI companies. The stable operation of Asian supply chains in turn supports the return expectations of global AI investment. This is a mutually reinforcing cycle, not a zero-sum game. The scale of this cycle is expanding rapidly. In recent years, global trade in AI-related products has grown far faster than overall merchandise trade. While AI-related goods may account for about 15 percent of world trade, trade in AI-enabling goods drove 42 percent of goods trade growth in 2025, and this share rose to 76 percent during the first quarter of 2026, according to World Trade Organization and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development analysis. Without the large-scale, cost-effective AI hardware provided by Asian supply chains, the cost of global data center construction would rise sharply, the pace of AI adoption would be far slower, and AI deployment in every country would ultimately suffer. Conversely, the rapid growth of Asia's AI industry has also created substantial new import demand, from high-end research and development equipment to specialized software in niche fields to AI service solutions adapted to different markets. This does not mean Asia can rest easy. Challenges such as geopolitical disruptions to supply chains, export controls on critical technologies, and bottlenecks in power and computing infrastructure could all affect the sustainability of this round of dividends. But for now, with the region's ability to capture the dividends of AI trade expansion, Asia has already secured a key position on that track.

item.title: Philippine military backs suspension of direct communication with China, raising risks of misjudgment, escalation: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 22:02:00
Defense Secretary of the Philippines Gilbert Teodoro Jr. File photo: VCG The Philippine military has thrown its support behind Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.'s suspension of direct military-to-military communication channels with China, as the Chinese Embassy in Manila warned that shutting down such contact fuels mistrust and narrows the space for crisis management amid continuing tensions in the South China Sea. The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) claimed Tuesday that it "stands solidly behind and firmly supports" Teodoro's move, according to a report from the Philippine News Agency on Tuesday. A Chinese expert noted that the suspension of military-to-military communications between China and the Philippines would further undermine dialogue and mutual trust, while increasing the risk of misjudging each other's intentions. In the context of frequent maritime encounters, such miscalculations could severely weaken crisis management, raise the likelihood of sudden or unintended incidents, and expose frontline personnel on both sides to greater risks if tensions escalate unexpectedly because of less available communication channels. The AFP spokesperson, retired Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, claimed communication mechanisms could only work when based on what he described as mutual trust, sincerity and support for international law. He claimed bilateral dialogue had failed because "the messages" did not match "the actions on sea, air and ground," and accused China of using direct communication as a "smokescreen," a report in the Philippine Star said on Wednesday. Trinidad also claimed that the AFP will continue to perform its sea patrol and "will keep performing rotation and resupply missions," according to the Philippine Star report. The Chinese Embassy in the Philippines, responding to the suspension, said "communication channels should remain open to avoid miscalculation and prevent tensions from escalating." The Embassy criticized Teodoro for shutting down military-to-military communication for "political self interests," warning that the move "fuels mistrust, narrows the space for crisis management, and pushes frontline personnel closer to confrontation," according to the Embassy's Facebook account. The current dispute indicates that the suspension did not begin this week. Coverage from Philippine-based media outlet the Daily Tribune said that Teodoro claimed on Tuesday that military-to-military communication with China had been suspended for nearly three years. In a May 2024 statement posted by the Philippine Department of National Defense, Teodoro said he had disallowed contact between the department and the Chinese Embassy since a courtesy call by then Chinese Ambassador Huang Xilian shortly after Teodoro took office in July 2023. Although China and the Philippines maintain other communication channels, they cannot fully replace direct military-to-military contact. Diplomatic channels are mainly used for broader policy and strategic coordination, while coast guard communication focuses more on specific maritime law enforcement. Military exchanges, by contrast, deal with more specialized and sensitive issues involving defense policy, military strategy and security concerns, Chen Xiangmiao, a research fellow at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, told the Global Times on Wednesday. Chen noted that military communication serves as an important "backstop" for bilateral relations. Even when serious differences exist in the South China Sea, direct military contact can help clarify strategic intentions and security red lines, preventing specific maritime incidents from escalating into broader military confrontations. Given that the Philippine military also plays a role in planning and directing some maritime operations, restoring effective military-to-military communication remains important if Manila genuinely wants to manage disputes and reduce risks, Chen said. The latest military position comes as the Marcos administration stresses that the president intends to maintain engagement with Beijing. Palace communications undersecretary Claire Castro said that Manila would continue engaging with China, particularly in trade and investment, a report from News Watch Plus Philippines on Tuesday shows. Just days earlier, Marcos said his "greatest fear" was that a mistake by a seaman or soldier could develop into "something that goes out of control," while stressing the importance of managing problems and preventing misunderstandings in the South China Sea. The expert pointed out that the Philippine government's position appears to be internally inconsistent: while the presidential palace stresses dialogue and maintaining normal engagement with China, the defense establishment supports suspending direct military communication. Cutting such a channel would not make the Philippines safer, but would further weaken trust, increase the risk of miscalculation and ultimately impose greater security and political costs on Manila. Chen said this reflects a "double-track" approach: Manila portrays itself as willing to communicate and maintain overall bilateral stability, while continuing actions in the South China Sea that undermine existing understandings and create new friction. If the Philippines genuinely wants to manage risks, it should stop provocative actions, return to dialogue and restore effective crisis-management channels, including military-to-military communication.

item.title: Europe, beware of Taiwan politician's self-serving 'warning'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 21:02:00
China-EU relationship Photo: VCG Certain forces of the Taiwan region are exploiting yet another international platform to peddle their separatist agenda, this time using a Western buzzword in Poland to drag the EU into its political stunts. According to media reports, Taiwan's "foreign minister" Lin Chia-lung, during a speech in Poland on Tuesday, warned the EU that dependence on Chinese suppliers poses a risk to the bloc's freedom. The remarks came as European leaders will gather in Brussels this week to weigh up the future of trading ties with China. Such remarks serve a number of ulterior motivations behind Taiwan politicians. First, Taiwan politicians harbor no genuine concern for the EU's interests, but only want to internationalize the Taiwan question by hijacking a major China-EU agenda, creating the false impression that Taiwan has a legitimate stake in Europe's trade and security decisions. Second, they aim to drive a wedge between China and the EU, exploiting Europe's internal debates on "de-risking" to sow suspicion and friction where none need exist. Third, they attempt to dress up a separatist agenda in the language of "freedom" and "values," borrowing Western slogans to lend their cause a veneer of legitimacy it does not deserve. After all, the one-China principle is a consensus of the international community and a norm governing international relations. As an inalienable part of China, Taiwan has no right - under any name, in any capacity, or on any international occasion - to issue so-called "warnings" or make pronouncements on China-EU relations. The EU's approach to China today is marked by a deep and unresolved ambivalence. On one hand, Brussels acknowledges the necessity of a "stable and balanced" trade relationship, recognizing that China remains an indispensable partner for Europe's economic and green transition goals. On the other hand, European institutions increasingly frame China as a "critical long-term strategic challenge," claiming it holds "asymmetric advantages" over the EU through its economic and technological dominance. Interdependence, once seen as a foundation for stability, is now treated as a source of vulnerability. This tension has driven the EU toward a policy of "de-risking," which in practice often looks less like prudent diversification and more like a deliberate effort to reduce dependence on Chinese suppliers across critical sectors. A case in point is that in June, the European Commission decided to propose a new law requiring EU companies to diversify their sources of key supplies, the focus of which, clearly, is China. With such measures as their policy tools, the EU is not protecting its freedom; it is eroding the very foundation of its prosperity. China has consistently supported a strong, united, and prosperous Europe. But if Brussels chooses to define its relationship with China through the lens of suspicion and adversarial posturing, it will find that the costs of derisking far outweigh the imagined risks of engagement. The timing of the so-called warning from the Taiwan politician is telling. It also came just days after EU and Chinese trade officials concluded their second Trade and Investment Consultations in Beijing, where both sides reached agreements on hybrid vehicle exports, rare earth supply channels, and market access. The EU should realize that the "warning" from Taiwan is nothing but a wolf in sheep's clothes. If European institutions allow such remarks to fester unchecked, or worse, use them as a pretext to advance the so-called "supply chain de-risking" agenda, it would mark a dangerous shift in Europe's trade policy - moving away from pragmatic cooperation and toward ideological confrontation. Such a move would only lend credibility to a separatist narrative that has no place in international affairs. If Brussels truly values strategic autonomy, it should resist the temptation to convert trade policy into an instrument of ideological posturing, and instead keep the China-EU relationship anchored in realism, reciprocity, and respect.

item.title: HYROX postpones Shanghai event over venue issues following a Beijing race hygiene controversy
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 20:00:00
Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia in action during the HYROX Beijing event at the National Speed Skating Oval in Beijing, China, on September 12, 2026. Photo: VCG Indoor fitness competition HYROX announced on Wednesday that its Shanghai event would be postponed because of unforeseen problems with venue arrangements. The indoor hybrid fitness endurance race had previously faced attention after a competitor experienced a bowel incident mid-race at HYROX Beijing. The HYROX Shanghai event, originally scheduled for October 31 to November 1, 2026, will be postponed, the organizer said on its official Sina Weibo account. The venue will remain unchanged. All purchased race entries and spectator tickets will automatically be transferred to the rescheduled event dates. Those unable to attend the rescheduled event may apply for a full refund, the organizer said. The HYROX China organizing committee apologized to athletes and spectators for postponing the Shanghai event, acknowledging that the decision had disrupted their training and travel plans. On September 12, Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk experienced bowel incontinence during the women’s pro race at the HYROX Beijing event, held at the National Speed Skating Oval in Beijing. She continued competing and won the women’s pro race. The incident sparked online criticism over its impact on racecourse hygiene, as well as questions about the organizers’ sanitation measures and on-site management. Several athletes withdrew from the HYROX Shanghai event following the bowel incontinence controversy at the Beijing event, citing concerns over hygiene and safety at future races. Some withdrawing athletes filed lawsuits over refund processing fees, Chao News, a media outlet under Zhejiang Daily, reported in September. Global Times
